Commit Messages: More Than Just Code Comments

Why clear commit messages matter, how Conventional Commits bring structure to project history, and practical ways to make changes easier to understand, review, and debug.

By Muhammad Ahsan Ali
GitConventional CommitsSoftware Engineering

Many developers wonder, “Why bother with commit messages? Who reads them anyway? Isn’t the code all that matters?” This thinking is flawed. Commit messages are crucial. When debugging, trying to understand why a specific line was written, or figuring out the logic behind a piece of code, these messages become invaluable. They help you grasp the potential impact of changing code on business logic.

Why Write Professional Commit Messages?

When you open a commit weeks or months later, do you remember exactly what changes you made and why? Most developers who make quick fixes often can’t recall the specifics behind vague messages like “update login flow”.

This leaves you in a dark room with no traceable history. You’re left wondering, “What if changing this line breaks a function or causes ripple effects on the business logic?” Without clear commit messages, you’re navigating blindly through your codebase.

Bad Commit Message vs. Good Commit Message

Let’s compare two approaches:

Bad Commit Message

update login flows

Good Commit Message

Create a new login page for team users

We want to capture team names in the login flow for paid users. This commit shows the new login page for users with a valid team ID.

Both commits relate to updating the login workflow, but the differences are stark. The first example merely states that the login flow was updated, offering no context or reasoning. The second example, however, explains the purpose behind the update and provides specific details about the changes.

Now, imagine you’re part of a team where people write commits like the first example. You’re stuck debugging an issue and need to understand why a particular change was made. Your first instinct is to check the commit message, hoping to find the developer’s reasoning. But you find it unhelpful and vague.

At this point, your only option is to make educated guesses about the business or development plan. This approach could lead to decisions that negatively impact the system. On the other hand, the second example clearly explains why the login workflow was updated, allowing you to make informed decisions about where to make changes while minimizing the impact on the development system.

This comparison highlights a crucial point: commit messages are the thread that connects developers across time and space. When a developer isn’t available to explain their code in person, their commit messages step in to provide that vital context.

The Power of Clear Communication

Clear commit messages serve several important purposes:

  1. Historical Context: They provide a chronological record of why changes were made, not just what changes occurred.
  2. Debugging Aid: When issues arise, good commit messages can quickly point developers to the root cause or at least provide clues about where to start looking.
  3. Onboarding Tool: New team members can get up to speed faster by reading through commit history to understand the project’s evolution.
  4. Decision Making: They help developers make informed decisions about future changes by understanding the reasoning behind past modifications.
  5. Code Review: Reviewers can better understand the intent behind changes, leading to more effective code reviews.
  6. Project Management: Clear commits can help project managers track progress and understand the scope of work completed.

What are Conventional Commits?

Conventional Commits offer a lightweight framework for structuring commit messages. This standardized format makes it easier to read and understand the purpose of each commit at a glance.

Basic Structure of Conventional Commits

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]

Let’s break down each component.

1. Type

This indicates the kind of change made. Common types include:

  • feat: A new feature
  • fix: A bug fix
  • docs: Documentation changes
  • style: Changes that don’t affect code meaning (white-space, formatting, etc.)
  • refactor: Code changes that neither fix a bug nor add a feature
  • perf: Changes that improve performance
  • test: Adding or correcting tests
  • chore: Changes to the build process or auxiliary tools

2. Optional scope

This specifies the part of the codebase the commit affects. It’s enclosed in parentheses and followed by a colon and space.

3. Description

A brief summary of the code changes. It should be written in the imperative mood, as if giving a command (e.g., “add feature” not “added feature”).

4. Optional body

A more detailed explanation of the changes, including the motivation for the change and contrasts with previous behavior.

5. Optional footer(s)

This section can include information about breaking changes and references to issue trackers.

Examples of Conventional Commits

Let’s look at some examples to illustrate how Conventional Commits work in practice:

1. Adding a new feature

feat(user-auth): implement two-factor authentication

- Add option for users to enable 2FA in their account settings
- Implement SMS-based verification code system
- Update login flow to accommodate 2FA checks

Closes #123

2. Fixing a bug

fix(api): resolve data inconsistency in user profile endpoint

The user profile endpoint was returning outdated information due to
incorrect cache invalidation. This commit updates the caching logic
to ensure fresh data is always returned.

Fixes #456

3. Refactoring code

refactor(database): optimize user search query

- Rewrite user search query to use indexing more effectively
- Reduce query execution time by approximately 40%
- No functional changes, only performance improvements

Performance tests: before: 1.2s, after: 0.7s

4. Updating documentation

docs: update API documentation for v2 endpoints

- Add detailed descriptions for all new v2 API endpoints
- Include request/response examples for each endpoint
- Update authentication section to reflect new token-based system

This update ensures our API documentation is current with the latest
changes introduced in the v2 release.

5. Breaking change

feat(api): migrate to GraphQL API

BREAKING CHANGE: This commit replaces our REST API with a new GraphQL API.
All clients will need to be updated to use the new query language.

- Implement GraphQL schema for existing data models
- Set up GraphQL server using Apollo
- Add authentication middleware for GraphQL endpoints

Migration guide: [link to migration doc]

Benefits of Using Conventional Commits

  1. Automatic Versioning: Tools can automatically determine the next semantic version number based on the types of commits.
  2. Automatic Changelog Generation: With structured commit messages, generating changelogs becomes a straightforward, automated process.
  3. Communication: They provide a standardised way for team members to communicate the nature and scope of changes.
  4. Easier Code Reviews: Reviewers can quickly understand the intent and scope of changes.
  5. Project History: They create a more readable and meaningful project history.

Best Practices for Writing Commit Messages

  1. Be Specific: Avoid vague messages like “fix bug” or “update code”. Provide context about what was changed and why.
  2. Keep it Concise: While the body can be longer, aim to keep the subject line under 50 characters.
  3. Use the Imperative Mood: Write as if you’re giving a command. For example, “fix” instead of “fixed” or “fixes”.
  4. Separate Subject from Body: Use a blank line to separate the subject from the body of the commit message.
  5. Explain the Why, Not Just the What: Your code shows what changed. Use the commit message to explain why the change was necessary.
  6. Reference Issues: If your commit relates to a specific issue or ticket, reference it in the commit message.
  7. Consider Your Future Self: Write messages that will help you understand the changes months or years from now.

Conclusion

Commit messages are the unsung heroes of code collaboration. They provide crucial context and clarity for future developers, including your future self. By adopting a professional approach to crafting commit messages, teams can streamline debugging processes, enhance code comprehension, and ultimately, boost development efficiency.

Conventional Commits offer a structured framework for ensuring consistency and effectiveness in message communication. This approach not only enhances team cohesion and productivity but also paves the way for automated versioning and changelog generation.

Remember, every commit message you write is a gift to future developers. It’s an investment in the long-term maintainability and understanding of your codebase. By taking the time to write clear, informative commit messages, you’re not just documenting changes — you’re telling the story of your project’s evolution, one commit at a time.
